claim: Circadian clocks are composed of transcription-translation negative feedback loops that pace rhythms of gene expression to the diurnal cycle.
source: Circadian clocks are composed of transcription-translation negative feedback loops that pace rhythms of gene expression to the diurnal cycle.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about circadian clocks.

claim: In Neurospora crassa, the proteins Frequency (FRQ), the FRQ-interacting RNA helicase (FRH), and Casein-Kinase I (CK1) form the FFC complex that represses expression of genes activated by the white-collar complex (WCC).
source: In the filamentous fungus Neurospora crassa, the proteins Frequency (FRQ), the FRQ-interacting RNA helicase (FRH), and Casein-Kinase I (CK1) form the FFC complex that represses expression of genes activated by the white-collar complex (WCC).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Neurospora circadian clock system.

claim: FRQ orchestrates key molecular interactions of the clock despite containing little predicted tertiary structure.
source: FRQ orchestrates key molecular interactions of the clock despite containing little predicted tertiary structure.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational predictions and experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: FRQ contains a compact core that associates and organizes FRH and CK1 to coordinate their roles in WCC repression.
source: FRQ contains a compact core that associates and organizes FRH and CK1 to coordinate their roles in WCC repression.
evidence: This is supported by DEER spectroscopy and SAXS data showing FRQ structure and FFC complex formation.

claim: FRQ phosphorylation increases conformational flexibility and alters oligomeric state, but the changes in structure and dynamics are non-uniform.
source: FRQ phosphorylation increases conformational flexibility and alters oligomeric state, but the changes in structure and dynamics are non-uniform.
evidence: This is supported by SAXS, SEC-MALS, and ESR data comparing phosphorylated and non-phosphorylated FRQ.

claim: Full-length FRQ undergoes liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS) to sequester FRH and CK1 and influence CK1 enzymatic activity.
source: Full-length FRQ undergoes liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS) to sequester FRH and CK1 and influence CK1 enzymatic activity.
evidence: This is supported by turbidity assays, microscopy, and phosphorylation assays showing LLPS and its effects.

claim: FRQ phosphorylation favors LLPS.
source: Although FRQ phosphorylation favors LLPS, LLPS feeds back to reduce FRQ phosphorylation by CK1 at higher temperatures.
evidence: This is supported by turbidity assays showing increased LLPS with phosphorylated FRQ.

claim: LLPS feeds back to reduce FRQ phosphorylation by CK1 at higher temperatures.
source: Although FRQ phosphorylation favors LLPS, LLPS feeds back to reduce FRQ phosphorylation by CK1 at higher temperatures.
evidence: This is supported by phosphorylation assays at different temperatures showing reduced FRQ phosphorylation under LLPS conditions.

claim: Live imaging of Neurospora hyphae reveals FRQ foci characteristic of condensates near the nuclear periphery.
source: Live imaging of Neurospora hyphae reveals FRQ foci characteristic of condensates near the nuclear periphery.
evidence: This is supported by live-cell imaging data showing FRQ-mNeonGreen foci in nuclei.

claim: Analogous clock repressor proteins in higher organisms share little position-specific sequence identity with FRQ.
source: Analogous clock repressor proteins in higher organisms share little position-specific sequence identity with FRQ; yet, they contain amino acid compositions that promote LLPS.
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis showing low sequence conservation but similar physicochemical properties.

claim: Analogous clock repressor proteins in higher organisms contain amino acid compositions that promote LLPS.
source: Analogous clock repressor proteins in higher organisms share little position-specific sequence identity with FRQ; yet, they contain amino acid compositions that promote LLPS.
evidence: This is supported by computational predictions of LLPS propensity for FRQ, dPER, and hPER1.

claim: Condensate formation may be a conserved feature of eukaryotic clocks.
source: Hence, condensate formation may be a conserved feature of eukaryotic clocks.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the LLPS propensity of clock repressor proteins across species.

claim: FRQ is functionally analogous to Period (PER) in insects and mammals.
source: FRQ is functionally analogous to Period (PER) in insects and mammals, whereas CK1 is an ortholog of the mammalian CK1 and the Drosophila kinase Doubletime (DBT) (Dunlap and Loros, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature.

claim: CK1 is an ortholog of the mammalian CK1 and the Drosophila kinase Doubletime (DBT).
source: FRQ is functionally analogous to Period (PER) in insects and mammals, whereas CK1 is an ortholog of the mammalian CK1 and the Drosophila kinase Doubletime (DBT) (Dunlap and Loros, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature.

claim: FRH is found only in the core repressor of the fungal clock.
source: FRH is found only in the core repressor of the fungal clock.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about the fungal clock.

claim: FRH is homologous to the yeast helicase MTR4.
source: Although FRH is homologous to the yeast helicase MTR4, FRH helicase activity does not appear essential to clock function (Conrad et al., 2016; Hurley et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature.

claim: FRH helicase activity does not appear essential to clock function.
source: Although FRH is homologous to the yeast helicase MTR4, FRH helicase activity does not appear essential to clock function (Conrad et al., 2016; Hurley et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: WCC binding to the clock-box (c-box) activates frq expression.
source: WCC binding to the clock-box (c-box) activates frq expression (Figure 1A; Froehlich et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: FRQ production is highly regulated at the post-transcriptional level through the use of rare codons to retard translation, the expression of an antisense transcript and alternative splicing mechanisms.
source: FRQ production is also highly regulated at the post-transcriptional level through the use of rare codons to retard translation, the expression of an antisense transcript and alternative splicing mechanisms (Cha et al., 2015; Dunlap and Loros, 2017; Zhou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature.

claim: Alternative splicing leads to the production of either a long (L-FRQ) or short (S-FRQ) isoform.
source: The latter leads to the production of either a long (L-FRQ) or short (S-FRQ) isoform, and the ratio of these isoforms fine-tunes period length in response to ambient temperatures (Diernfellner et al., 2007; Liu et al., 1997; Zhou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature.

claim: The ratio of L-FRQ and S-FRQ isoforms fine-tunes period length in response to ambient temperatures.
source: The latter leads to the production of either a long (L-FRQ) or short (S-FRQ) isoform, and the ratio of these isoforms fine-tunes period length in response to ambient temperatures (Diernfellner et al., 2007; Liu et al., 1997; Zhou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature.

claim: Translated FRQ binds to FRH via its FFD domain.
source: Translated FRQ binds to FRH via its FFD domain and to CK1 via its two FCD domains (1 and 2) to form the repressive FFC (Cha et al., 2015; Dunlap and Loros, 2017; Jankowski et al., 2022; Figure 1C), although short linear motifs within FRQ may also broadly influence the FRQ-interactome (Pelham et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: FRQ binds to CK1 via its two FCD domains (1 and 2).
source: Translated FRQ binds to FRH via its FFD domain and to CK1 via its two FCD domains (1 and 2) to form the repressive FFC (Cha et al., 2015; Dunlap and Loros, 2017; Jankowski et al., 2022; Figure 1C), although short linear motifs within FRQ may also broadly influence the FRQ-interactome (Pelham et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: Short linear motifs within FRQ may broadly influence the FRQ-interactome.
source: Translated FRQ binds to FRH via its FFD domain and to CK1 via its two FCD domains (1 and 2) to form the repressive FFC (Cha et al., 2015; Dunlap and Loros, 2017; Jankowski et al., 2022; Figure 1C), although short linear motifs within FRQ may also broadly influence the FRQ-interactome (Pelham et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: The FFC enters the nucleus where it directly inhibits the WCC and thereby downregulates frq expression.
source: The FFC enters the nucleus where it directly inhibits the WCC and thereby downregulates frq expression (Hurley et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature.

claim: FRQ-mediated WCC phosphorylation by CK1 (and associated kinases) reduces interactions between the WCC and the c-box to close the feedback loop and restart the cycle.
source: FRQ-mediated WCC phosphorylation by CK1 (and associated kinases) reduces interactions between the WCC and the c-box to close the feedback loop and restart the cycle (Figure 1A; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: FRH facilitates interactions between the FFC and the WCC.
source: FRH facilitates interactions between the FFC and the WCC (Conrad et al., 2016), and thus, repressor function likely depends upon the FRQ-mediated association of CK1 and FRH.
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Repressor function likely depends upon the FRQ-mediated association of CK1 and FRH.
source: FRH facilitates interactions between the FFC and the WCC (Conrad et al., 2016), and thus, repressor function likely depends upon the FRQ-mediated association of CK1 and FRH.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited literature.

claim: Core negative arm proteins across species share low-sequence conservation.
source: Despite low-sequence conservation among the core negative arm proteins across species, they all share a high degree of disorder (Pelham et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Core negative arm proteins across species share a high degree of disorder.
source: Despite low-sequence conservation among the core negative arm proteins across species, they all share a high degree of disorder (Pelham et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: FRQ has >65% disorder predicted in its sequence with ~86% of the FRQ sequence assumed to have no defined structure.
source: FRQ, the analogous Drosophila (d) Period (PER) protein, and the analogous mammalian (m) PER have >65% disorder predicted in their sequences with ~86% of the FRQ sequence assumed to have no defined structure (Pelham et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Both FRQ and mPER2 have biochemical properties characteristic of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs).
source: Both FRQ and mPER2 have biochemical properties characteristic of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) (Hurley et al., 2013; Marzoll et al., 2022).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Clock repressors undergo extensive post-translational modification (PTM), particularly phosphorylation.
source: These clock repressors also undergo extensive post-translational modification (PTM), particularly phosphorylation (Dunlap and Loros, 2018; Pelham et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: FRQ acquires over 100 phosphorylation sites over the course of the circadian day, predominantly due to CK1.
source: FRQ acquires over 100 phosphorylation sites over the course of the circadian day (similar to PER phosphorylation by DBT), predominantly due to CK1 (Baker et al., 2009; Tang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Phosphorylation events weaken the interaction between FRQ and the WCC or CK1.
source: The phosphorylation events have two consequences: (1) those that weaken the interaction between FRQ and the WCC or CK1 (Cha et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2019) and (2) those that direct FRQ down the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway (Larrondo et al., 2015), although only the former are required for circadian rhythmicity (Larrondo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Phosphorylation events direct FRQ down the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway.
source: The phosphorylation events have two consequences: (1) those that weaken the interaction between FRQ and the WCC or CK1 (Cha et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2019) and (2) those that direct FRQ down the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway (Larrondo et al., 2015), although only the former are required for circadian rhythmicity (Larrondo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Only phosphorylation events that weaken FRQ-WCC or FRQ-CK1 interactions are required for circadian rhythmicity.
source: The phosphorylation events have two consequences: (1) those that weaken the interaction between FRQ and the WCC or CK1 (Cha et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2019) and (2) those that direct FRQ down the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway (Larrondo et al., 2015), although only the former are required for circadian rhythmicity (Larrondo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Multisite phosphorylation of FRQ influences its inhibitory function and clock period length.
source: Multisite phosphorylation of FRQ influences its inhibitory function and clock period length (Larrondo et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: IDPs such as FRQ are known to participate in liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS).
source: IDPs such as FRQ are known to participate in liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS), which has emerged as a key mechanism for organizing cellular components, coordinating metabolism and directing signaling through, for example, the formation of membraneless organelles (MLOs) (Dignon et al., 2020; Wright and Dyson, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature.

claim: LLPS has emerged as a key mechanism for organizing cellular components, coordinating metabolism and directing signaling through the formation of membraneless organelles (MLOs).
source: IDPs such as FRQ are known to participate in liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS), which has emerged as a key mechanism for organizing cellular components, coordinating metabolism and directing signaling through, for example, the formation of membraneless organelles (MLOs) (Dignon et al., 2020; Wright and Dyson, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature.

claim: Emerging studies in plants, flies, and cyanobacteria implicate LLPS in circadian clocks.
source: Emerging studies in plants (Jung et al., 2020), flies (Xiao et al., 2021), and cyanobacteria (Cohen et al., 2014; Pattanayak et al., 2020) implicate LLPS in circadian clocks, and in Neurospora it has recently been shown that the Period-2 (PRD-2) RNA-binding protein influences frq mRNA localization through a mechanism potentially mediated by LLPS (Bartholomai, 2022a).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: In Neurospora, the Period-2 (PRD-2) RNA-binding protein influences frq mRNA localization through a mechanism potentially mediated by LLPS.
source: Emerging studies in plants (Jung et al., 2020), flies (Xiao et al., 2021), and cyanobacteria (Cohen et al., 2014; Pattanayak et al., 2020) implicate LLPS in circadian clocks, and in Neurospora it has recently been shown that the Period-2 (PRD-2) RNA-binding protein influences frq mRNA localization through a mechanism potentially mediated by LLPS (Bartholomai, 2022a).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Analysis of an AlphaFold 2.0 model of full-length FRQ indicates that FRQ lacks a defined arrangement of large folded domains.
source: Analysis of an AlphaFold 2.0 (Jumper et al., 2021) model of full-length FRQ indicates that FRQ lacks a defined arrangement of large folded domains; instead, most of the molecule is unstructured (Figure 1B), in agreement with previous studies predicting that FRQ mostly comprises intrinsically disordered regions (Hurley et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on computational modeling using AlphaFold 2.0.

claim: Most of the FRQ molecule is unstructured according to AlphaFold 2.0 modeling.
source: Analysis of an AlphaFold 2.0 (Jumper et al., 2021) model of full-length FRQ indicates that FRQ lacks a defined arrangement of large folded domains; instead, most of the molecule is unstructured (Figure 1B), in agreement with previous studies predicting that FRQ mostly comprises intrinsically disordered regions (Hurley et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on computational modeling using AlphaFold 2.0.

claim: FRQ is predicted to contain a small, clustered core, with several secondary structural elements that collapse together to form a compact nucleus surrounded by long flexible disordered regions.
source: However, FRQ is also predicted to contain a small, clustered core, with several secondary structural elements that collapse together to form a compact nucleus surrounded by long flexible disordered regions (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on computational modeling using AlphaFold 2.0.

claim: The AlphaFold pLDDT scores are very low across the FRQ model, except within the core.
source: The AlphaFold pLDDT scores, which represent the confidence in the structural prediction (Jumper et al., 2021), are very low across the model, except within the core (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which contains the CK1-binding region.
evidence: This is based on computational modeling using AlphaFold 2.0.

claim: The FRQ core contains the CK1-binding region.
source: The AlphaFold pLDDT scores, which represent the confidence in the structural prediction (Jumper et al., 2021), are very low across the model, except within the core (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which contains the CK1-binding region.
evidence: This is based on computational modeling using AlphaFold 2.0.

claim: The FRH-binding region, FFD, falls within a more flexible region with a lower pLDDT score than that of CK1.
source: The FRH-binding region, FFD, falls within a more flexible region with a lower pLDDT score than that of CK1.
evidence: This is based on computational modeling using AlphaFold 2.0.

claim: Helices compose the majority of secondary structural elements predicted by AlphaFold for FRQ.
source: Helices compose the majority of secondary structural elements predicted by AlphaFold (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on computational modeling using AlphaFold 2.0.

claim: The assignments of the helical regions in FRQ were well supported by the Agadir program that predicts helical propensity based on the helix/coil transition theory.
source: The assignments of the helical regions were well supported by the Agadir program that predicts helical propensity based on the helix/coil transition theory (Muñoz and Serrano, 1994).
evidence: This is based on computational prediction using the Agadir program.

claim: Four regions distributed throughout the length of FRQ (residues 194–212, 312–329, 709–719, and 801–817) have at least 10% helical propensity.
source: Four regions distributed throughout the length of FRQ (residues 194–212, 312–329, 709–719, and 801–817) have at least 10% helical propensity, and these helical regions mostly agree with those of the AlphaFold model (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on computational prediction using the Agadir program.

claim: FRQ assumes a broad conformational ensemble containing an ordered nucleus that interacts extensively with partially ordered and flexible regions.
source: Together, these analyses primarily indicate that FRQ assumes a broad conformational ensemble containing an ordered nucleus that interacts extensively with partially ordered and flexible regions.
evidence: This is an inference based on computational predictions from AlphaFold and Agadir.

claim: The size and intrinsic disorder of FRQ have made it challenging to recombinantly express and purify.
source: The size and intrinsic disorder of FRQ have made it challenging to recombinantly express and purify, thereby limiting investigations of its biophysical properties.
evidence: This is a statement about the challenges faced in the study.

claim: Previous purifications have characterized FRQ as an IDP, but suffered from low yields and aggregated species.
source: Previous purifications have characterized FRQ as an IDP, but suffered from low yields and aggregated species (Hurley et al., 2013; Lauinger et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Methods proven effective for IDPs yielded comparatively well-behaved FRQ protein.
source: We also encountered extensive protein degradation and aggregation with conventional purification methods and affinity-tagging strategies; however, methods proven effective for IDPs (Pedersen et al., 2020) yielded comparatively well-behaved protein.
evidence: This is based on experimental methods applied in the study.

claim: Nickel affinity chromatography and size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) under denaturing conditions were carried out to maximize yield and reduce aggregation of full-length L-FRQ.
source: Briefly, we carried out nickel affinity chromatography and size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) under denaturing conditions to maximize yield and reduce aggregation of full-length L-FRQ (residues 1–989; Figure 2A; Seal et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used.

claim: Solubilization with high concentrations of guanidinium-HCl prevented proteolysis, aggregation, and limited co-purification of impurities.
source: Solubilization with high concentrations of guanidinium-HCl prevented proteolysis, aggregation, and limited co-purification of impurities that were otherwise difficult to remove.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used.

claim: Once FRQ was isolated, the protein remained soluble, monodisperse, and could be concentrated after the denaturant was removed by dialysis.
source: Once FRQ was isolated, the protein remained soluble, monodisperse, and could be concentrated after the denaturant was removed by dialysis (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This describes the experimental results.

claim: FRQ is one of the largest native IDPs produced in amounts amenable to structural and biophysical characterization.
source: To our knowledge, FRQ is one of the largest native IDPs produced in amounts amenable to structural and biophysical characterization.
evidence: This is a statement about the significance of the work.

claim: To generate phosphorylated FRQ, the protein was co-expressed with (untagged) CK1, which forms a stable complex with FRQ and acts as its primary kinase.
source: To generate phosphorylated FRQ, the protein was co-expressed with (untagged) CK1, which forms a stable complex with FRQ and acts as its primary kinase (Querfurth et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used.

claim: Phosphorylation of FRQ was confirmed visually by altered migration on SDS-PAGE and mass spectrometry.
source: Phosphorylation was confirmed visually by altered migration on SDS-PAGE (Figure 2A) and mass spectrometry (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes the experimental results.

claim: Mass spectrometry revealed a network of >80 phosphorylation sites in phosphorylated FRQ.
source: The latter revealed a network of >80 phosphorylation sites (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), most of which agree with those found on natively expressed FRQ (Baker et al., 2009; Tang et al., 2009).
evidence: This describes the experimental results.

claim: Most of the phosphorylation sites in recombinant phosphorylated FRQ agree with those found on natively expressed FRQ.
source: The latter revealed a network of >80 phosphorylation sites (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), most of which agree with those found on natively expressed FRQ (Baker et al., 2009; Tang et al., 2009).
evidence: This describes the experimental results and comparison with literature.

claim: Co-expression of FRQ with CK1 increased protein yield and stability, while limiting aggregation and degradation.
source: In general, we found that co-expression of FRQ with CK1 increased protein yield and stability, while limiting aggregation and degradation.
evidence: This describes the experimental observations.

claim: SEC-MALS of p-FRQ gives a molecular weight measurement consistent with a primarily monomeric state (molecular weight [MW] of ~143 kDa versus a predicted MW of ~110 kDa).
source: Size-exclusion chromatography coupled to multiangle light scattering (SEC-MALS) of p-FRQ gives a molecular weight measurement consistent with a primarily monomeric state (molecular weight [MW] of ~143 kDa versus a predicted MW of ~110 kDa; Figure 2B).
evidence: This describes the experimental results from SEC-MALS.

claim: np-FRQ measured by MALS indicates a dimer and its measured mass distribution increases upon concentration.
source: In contrast, the np-FRQ measured by MALS indicates a dimer and its measured mass distribution increases upon concentration (Figure 2B)
evidence: This describes the experimental results from SEC-MALS.

claim: Purified np-FRQ dimerizes, whereas phosphorylation destabilizes this association.
source: Hence, purified np-FRQ dimerizes, whereas phosphorylation destabilizes this association.
evidence: This is an inference based on SEC-MALS data.

claim: SEC-coupled small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) analyses revealed that both p-FRQ and np-FRQ shared characteristics of highly flexible proteins, but that p-FRQ was more extended than np-FRQ.
source: SEC-coupled small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) analyses revealed that both p-FRQ and np-FRQ shared characteristics of highly flexible proteins, but that p-FRQ was more extended than np-FRQ (Table 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental results from SAXS.

claim: The dimensionless Kratky plots of p-FRQ and np-FRQ revealed high degrees of flexibility for both proteins.
source: The dimensionless Kratky plots of p-FRQ and np-FRQ, which report on compactness and conformational dispersity (Durand et al., 2010; Martin et al., 2021Bateman et al., 2021; Sagar et al., 2020; Trewhella et al., 2017), revealed high degrees of flexibility for both proteins (Figure 2C).
evidence: This describes the experimental results from SAXS.

claim: The peak values of the Kratky plot were shifted from those expected for compact structures but were also not indicative of fully disordered proteins.
source: The peak values of the plot were shifted from those expected for compact structures but were also not indicative of fully disordered proteins (Durand et al., 2010; Rambo and Tainer, 2011; Sagar et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the experimental results from SAXS.

claim: p-FRQ appears more disordered than np-FRQ, a characteristic also reflected in their pairwise distance distributions.
source: Furthermore, p-FRQ appears more disordered than np-FRQ, a characteristic also reflected in their pairwise distance distributions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental results from SAXS.

claim: FRQ generally adopts a relatively monodisperse conformational state that is partially compact but highly flexible and then increases expanse and flexibility upon phosphorylation.
source: These data then indicate that FRQ generally adopts a relatively monodisperse conformational state that is partially compact but highly flexible and then increases expanse and flexibility upon phosphorylation.
evidence: This is an inference based on SAXS and SEC-MALS data.

claim: This general picture is consistent with the increased susceptibility to proteolysis that FRQ experiences with phosphorylation.
source: This general picture is consistent with the increased susceptibility to proteolysis that FRQ experiences with phosphorylation (Liu et al., 2019; Srivastava and Freed, 2019; Pelham et al., 2020; Querfurth et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data and cited literature.

claim: FRQ has four native cysteine residues that provide reactive sites for nitroxide spin labels (SLs).
source: FRQ has four native cysteine residues that provide reactive sites for nitroxide spin labels (SLs) (Figure 3A and B; Berliner et al., 1982).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach.

claim: The Cys residues distribute relatively evenly throughout the FRQ protein sequence and fall within areas of varying structural order that include the binding regions for the core clock proteins (FRH, CK1, WC1, and WC2).
source: The Cys residues distribute relatively evenly throughout the protein sequence and fall within areas of varying structural order that include the binding regions for the core clock proteins (FRH, CK1, WC1, and WC2; Tables 2 and 3, Figure 3B).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach and sequence analysis.

claim: Enzymatic SortaseA and AEP1 peptide-coupling methods were developed and applied to spin-label FRQ at its N- and C- termini.
source: Furthermore, we developed and applied enzymatic SortaseA and AEP1 peptide-coupling methods (Chandrasekaran et al., 2021; Nguyen et al., 2015) to spin-label FRQ at its N- and C- termini (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods developed.

claim: cw-ESR reveals that FRQ has regions of varying order that agree with computational predictions.
source: cw-ESR reveals that FRQ has regions of varying order that agree with computational predictions and that some of these sites undergo phosphorylation-dependent conformational changes (Figure 3C).

claim: Some FRQ sites undergo phosphorylation-dependent conformational changes.
source: cw-ESR reveals that FRQ has regions of varying order that agree with computational predictions and that some of these sites undergo phosphorylation-dependent conformational changes (Figure 3C).
evidence: This describes the experimental results from cw-ESR.

claim: SLs attached to Cys490 and Cys658 (490SL and 658SL) are predicted to be within an α-helix and a β-strand, respectively.
source: SLs attached to Cys490 and Cys658 (490SL and 658SL) are predicted to be within an α-helix and a β-strand, respectively.
evidence: This is based on computational predictions.

source: These sites correspondingly showed a broad low-field (left-most line) component and a small high-field component (right-most line) indicative of slower tumbling compared to sites predicted to be in flexible regions, such as 746SL (Figure 3C).

claim: The 490SL site had a broader profile compared to that of the 658SL site, although both are relatively well ordered.
source: The 490SL site had a broader profile compared to that of the 658SL site, although both are relatively well ordered.
evidence: This describes the experimental results from cw-ESR.

claim: p-FRQ and np-FRQ gave very different δ values at 490SL and the C-terminus, demonstrating how phosphorylation can influence conformational properties site specifically.
source: Furthermore, the spectra also highlighted structural differences between the phospho forms: p-FRQ and np-FRQ gave very different δ values at 490SL and the C-terminus, thereby demonstrating how phosphorylation can influence conformational properties site specifically.
evidence: This describes the experimental results from cw-ESR.

claim: The C-terminus may have become more dynamic in p-FRQ compared to np-FRQ because the C-terminus contains a cluster of phosphosites.
source: The C-terminus may have become more dynamic in p-FRQ compared to np-FRQ because the C-terminus contains a cluster of phosphosites (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an inference based on cw-ESR data and sequence analysis.

claim: 490SL, which locates to the CK1-interaction region of the FCD2 domain, is more ordered in p-FRQ.
source: In contrast, the N-terminus and especially 490SL, which locates to the CK1-interaction region of the FCD2 domain, are more ordered in p-FRQ.
evidence: This describes the experimental results from cw-ESR.

claim: Differences in mobility between p-FRQ and np-FRQ in the FCD (490SL) may reflect changes in FRQ:CK1 interactions as FRQ becomes progressively phosphorylated across the circadian period.
source: Such differences in mobility between p-FRQ and np-FRQ in the FCD (490SL) may reflect changes in FRQ:CK1 interactions as FRQ becomes progressively phosphorylated across the circadian period (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference based on cw-ESR data and cited literature.

claim: np-FRQ was not amenable to DEER measurements owing to association and aggregation when concentrated.
source: Owing to association and aggregation when concentrated, np-FRQ was not amenable to DEER measurements; however, such issues were not prohibitive with p-FRQ.
evidence: This describes the experimental challenges.

claim: The modulation depths of the DEER data for p-FRQ are small (~2–4%), which compare to ~10–12% for a well-ordered, highly labeled pair of sites under these instrument conditions.
source: Nevertheless, due to the challenges of spin-labeling appreciable concentrations of p-FRQ, the modulation depths of the DEER data, which reflect the number of spins in range to produce specific dipolar interactions, are small (~2–4%).
